q.ruido: How much noise does it make, and how far from the neighbour?
q.espacio: How much space do I actually need?
q.mantenimiento: What maintenance does it need each year?

a.licencia: In most municipalities an uncovered court falls under minor works consent; a covered one usually needs full permission. We'll tell you what your local council requires and prepare the technical documentation.
a.ruido: Padel makes ball and voice noise, especially at night. Leaving around 3 m to the boundaries and facing the back walls towards your own plot is advisable; in sensitive cases we fit solutions that cut the nuisance.
a.espacio: The doubles court takes 20 × 10 m, but you have to count the maintenance perimeter: in practice, allow around 21 × 11 m. Singles drops to 20 × 6 m.
a.plazo: From signing, a standard court is usually ready in 4 to 6 weeks if the ground holds no surprises. The slab needs its curing time: rushing it compromises the build.
a.mantenimiento: Not much: brushing the turf and topping up the silica sand once or twice a year, plus a check of the fixings and glass. Turf replacement comes at around 8-10 years depending on use.

meta.title: How a padel court is built | Pádel Albufera
meta.description: From groundwork to the first ball: the 6 construction phases of a padel court, with the real thicknesses, dimensions and materials we use.

hero.h1: From bare ground to the first ball
hero.sub: Six construction phases, carried out by our own crew. This is what happens underneath the court, and why it matters more than it looks.

solera.titulo: It all comes down to the slab
solera.texto: A padel court is a steel-and-glass kit mounted on a concrete slab. Anyone can sell the kit; the slab is another matter. If the slab settles unevenly, the structure goes out of true, the doors stop closing and the glass works in torsion. Concrete flooring is where we come from: it's the part we know best and the one we don't subcontract.
solera.dato2d: Calculated so water clears on its own and the turf doesn't pool.
solera.dato3d: Concrete needs its time. Rushing it compromises the whole job.

fases.d: We set the court out on the ground and check orientation, access and water run-off. We excavate, strip the topsoil and compact the base in layers. Poorly compacted fill is the number one cause of settlement years down the line.

Formwork, mesh and pour. The surface is power-floated to leave it flat and even, with the planned fall for drainage. The lighting ducts go in at this point too: cutting chases afterwards means doing the work twice.
fases.dato: ≥ 15 cm with welded mesh and drainage fall

fases.d: Posts, beams and frames in galvanised steel with an epoxy finish in the chosen RAL colour. Each piece is plumbed and levelled before tightening: glass does not forgive an out-of-square structure.
fases.dato: Galvanised steel + epoxy, RAL chart colour

fases.d: Panels of 10 or 12 mm with polished edges, mounted on fixings with clearance so the glass can move. The back walls carry 3 m of glass topped with mesh up to 4 m; the sides are stepped.

The turf is laid, the rolls are joined with glued seams and the lines are set out. Then comes the silica sand, brushed in over several passes: that's what gives the correct bounce and holds the fibre upright. A freshly sanded court needs a few days of play to settle.
fases.dato: 5 cm lines · service line 6.95 m from the net

fases.d: LED floodlights are fitted, the net is tensioned and we walk the court with you for the final check. Heights, clearances and door closing are all verified before the job is signed off.
fases.dato: 10 m net: 0.88 m at the centre, 0.92 m at the posts
